entries.title: Menstruation
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: The menstrual cycle is the monthly process the body goes through to prepare for pregnancy. It is counted from the first day of one period to the first day of the next. Most menstrual cycles last about 28 days, but cycles can be shorter or longer and still be normal.

entries.title: Menstruation
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
topics: how long does a period last
entries.text: Most girls start having a period between ages 9 and 15, but some may start earlier or later. A period usually lasts three to seven days and can be light or heavy. It may take a few years to become regular. Your period may change during times that affect hormones, such as after childbirth or while breastfeeding. Periods usually continue until menopause, which most often happens between ages 45 and 55.

entries.title: Puberty
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Puberty is the time in life when a boy or girl becomes sexually mature. It is a process that usually happens between ages 8 and 13 for girls and ages 9 and 14 for boys. It causes physical changes and affects boys and girls differently. In girls: The first sign of puberty is usually breast development. Then hair grows in the pubic area and armpits. Menstruation (or a period) usually happens last.

entries.title: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), also known as polyendocrine metabolic ovary syndrome (PMOS), is the name of a hormonal disorder. PCOS affects the ovaries, as well as many other parts of the body. If you have PCOS, you usually have at least two of these problems: Not ovulating. Normally, your ovaries make the egg that is released each month as part of a healthy menstrual cycle. This is called ovulation. But with PCOS, the egg may not develop as it should, or it may not be released during ovulation. Your periods may be irregular, or you may not have them at all.

entries.title: Endometriosis
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Endometriosis is a disease in which tissue like the lining of the uterus grows in other places in your body. These patches of tissue are called "implants," "nodules," or "lesions." They are most often found: On or under the ovaries On the fallopian tubes, which carry eggs from the ovaries to the uterus Behind the uterus On the tissues that hold the uterus in place On the bowels or bladder

entries.title: Uterine Fibroids
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Uterine fibroids are the most common noncancerous (benign) tumors in women of childbearing age. You may have uterine fibroids and not even know it since they often don't cause any symptoms. Fibroids are made of muscle cells and other tissues that grow in and around the wall of the uterus, or womb. They can vary in number and size and grow as one tumor or in clusters.

entries.title: Premenstrual Syndrome
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Premenstrual syndrome, or PMS, is a group of physical and emotional symptoms that start one to two weeks before your period. Most women have at least some symptoms of PMS, and the symptoms go away after their periods start. The symptoms may range from mild to severe. What is premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD)? Premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) is a severe type of PMS. With PMDD, the symptoms are severe enough to interfere with your life. PMDD much less common than PMS.

entries.title: Thyroid Diseases
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Your thyroid is a small, butterfly-shaped gland in the front of your neck. It makes hormones that control the way the body uses energy. These hormones affect nearly every organ in your body and control many of your body's most important functions. For example, they affect your breathing, heart rate, weight, digestion, and moods. Thyroid diseases cause your thyroid to make either too much or too little of the hormones. Some of the different thyroid diseases include: Goiter, an enlargement of the thyroid gland Hyperthyroidism, which happens when your thyroid gland makes more thyroid hormones than your body needs Hypothyroidism, which happens when your thyroid gland does not make enough thyroid hormones

entries.title: Vaginitis
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Vaginitis, also called vulvovaginitis, is an inflammation or infection of the vagina. It can also affect the vulva, which is the external part of a woman's genitals. Vaginitis can cause itching, pain, discharge, and odor. Vaginitis is common, especially in women in their reproductive years. It usually happens when there is a change in the balance of bacteria or yeast that are normally found in your vagina. There are different types of vaginitis, and they have different causes, symptoms, and treatments.

entries.title: Menopause
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Menopause is the time in your life when you stop having your period and can no longer get pregnant. You have reached menopause when you have not had a period for 12 months. The time leading up to menopause is called the menopausal transition, or perimenopause. This transition usually begins when you are in your 40s, but sometimes it can start earlier. It can last for several years. The most common age for reaching menopause is between 45 and 55 years old.

entries.title: Menopause
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Early and premature menopause happens when your ovaries stop making hormones and your periods stop at a younger age than usual. When menopause happens before age 40, it's called premature menopause. If menopause happens before age 45, it's called early menopause.

entries.title: Primary Ovarian Insufficiency
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Primary ovarian insufficiency (POI) happens when your ovaries stop working normally before you are 40. As you get older, fertility naturally decreases. This usually starts around age 40 or later. Menstrual periods may also become irregular as you transition to menopause. If you have POI, these changes happen earlier, before age 40. Sometimes POI can start as early as the teenage years.

entries.title: Anemia
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: If you have anemia, your blood does not carry enough oxygen to the rest of your body. The most common cause of anemia is not having enough iron. Your body needs iron to make hemoglobin. Hemoglobin is an iron-rich protein that gives the red color to blood. It carries oxygen from the lungs to the rest of the body. Anemia has three main causes: blood loss, lack of red blood cell production, and high rates of red blood cell destruction.

entries.title: Sleep Disorders
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: While you are sleeping your brain and body functions are still active. Sleep is a natural process that helps your body restore energy, supports learning and memory, and keeps you healthy. It's not just the number of hours of sleep you get that matters. The quality of your sleep is also important. During the night, your brain cycles through different stages of non-rapid eye movement (non-REM) sleep and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. If your sleep is often interrupted, you may not get enough time in certain stages of sleep. Poor-quality sleep does more than make you feel tired. It can affect your physical and mental health, thinking, and daily functioning.

entries.title: Fatigue
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Fatigue is a feeling of weariness, tiredness, or lack of energy. It can interfere with your usual daily activities. Fatigue can be a normal response to physical activity, emotional stress, boredom, or lack of sleep. But sometimes it can be a sign of a mental or physical condition. If you have been feeling tired for weeks, contact your health care provider.

entries.title: Your menstrual cycle
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: A menstrual cycle begins with the first day of your period, or menstruation [MEN-stroo-AY-shuhn] and starts over again when the next period begins. Throughout a monthly menstrual cycle, your body makes different amounts of chemicals called hormones to prepare for pregnancy. These changing hormone levels can cause menstrual symptoms. Menstrual cycles often change as a woman gets older. A normal cycle lasts between 24 and 38 days.

entries.title: Period problems
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Your period lasts longer than eight days. You bleed through one or more pads or tampons every one to two hours. You feel dizzy, lightheaded, weak, or tired, or if you have chest pain or trouble breathing during or after your period. These can be symptoms of anemia.

entries.title: Polycystic ovary syndrome
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a health problem that affects 1 in 10 women of childbearing age. Women with PCOS have a hormonal imbalance and metabolism problems that may affect their overall health and appearance. PCOS is also a common and treatable cause of infertility.

entries.title: Menopause basics
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: You reach menopause after 12 months in a row with no period, including no spotting. After menopause, your ovaries make very little estrogen and progesterone, and they stop releasing eggs. The transition into menopause usually happens between ages 45 and 55. In the United States, the average age of menopause is 52.

entries.title: Menopause symptoms and relief
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Menopause symptoms go beyond hot flashes. They can affect your sleep, thinking, mood, joints, and bladder and genital health. Treatments can help. What symptoms can you have? Symptoms can begin in perimenopause. They can be mild, moderate, or severe. You may have: Not feeling like yourself (NFLM) Hot flashes and night sweats Sleep problems Brain fog and memory changes Mood changes, anxiety, and depression Joint and muscle pain Genital and urinary symptoms, called genitourinary syndrome of menopause (GSM) Changes in your periods Changes in sexual desire

entries.title: Menopause symptoms and relief
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Lower levels of estrogen can affect the tissues of your vagina, vulva, bladder, and urinary tract. Health care providers call this genitourinary syndrome of menopause, or GSM. Symptoms include repeat urinary tract infections (UTIs); pain during sex; burning, itching, or irritation of the vagina and vulva; a sudden or frequent need to urinate; and vaginal dryness.

entries.title: Early or premature menopause
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Menopause between ages 40 and 44 is early menopause. Menopause before age 40 is premature menopause, also called primary ovarian insufficiency (POI). Treatment can help relieve symptoms and protect your bones. What is the difference between early and premature menopause? Early menopause happens between ages 40 and 44. Premature menopause happens before age 40. Both can happen on their own or after medical treatment, such as surgery to remove both ovaries.

entries.title: Bacterial vaginosis
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Bacterial vaginosis (BV) is a condition caused by changes in the amount of certain types of bacteria in your vagina. BV is common, and any woman can get it. BV is easily treatable with medicine from your doctor or nurse. If left untreated, it can raise your risk for sexually transmitted infections (STIs) and cause problems during pregnancy.

entries.title: Vaginal yeast infections
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Most women will get a vaginal yeast infection at some point in their life. Symptoms of vaginal yeast infections include burning, itching, and thick, white discharge. Yeast infections are easy to treat, but it is important to see your doctor or nurse if you think you have an infection. Yeast infection symptoms are similar to other vaginal infections and sexually transmitted infections (STIs).

entries.title: Thyroid disease
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Problems with your menstrual period. Your thyroid helps control your menstrual cycle. Too much or too little thyroid hormone can make your periods very light, heavy, or irregular. Thyroid disease also can cause your periods to stop for several months or longer, a condition called amenorrhea.

entries.title: Iron-deficiency anemia
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Iron-deficiency anemia means that your body does not have enough iron. Your body needs iron to help carry oxygen through your blood to all parts of your body. Iron-deficiency anemia affects more women than men and is more common during pregnancy.

entries.title: Migraine
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: More than half of migraines in women occur right before, during, or after a woman has her period. This often is called "menstrual migraine." But, just a small fraction of women who have migraine around their period only have migraine at this time. Most have migraine headaches at other times of the month as well. How the menstrual cycle and migraine are linked is still unclear. We know that just before the cycle begins, levels of the female hormones, estrogen and progesterone, go down sharply. This drop in hormones may trigger a migraine, because estrogen controls chemicals in the brain that affect a woman's pain sensation.

entries.title: Amenorrhea
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Amenorrhea (pronounced ey-men-uh-REE-uh or uh-men-uh-REE-uh) is the medical term for the lack of a menstrual period. Amenorrhea is not a disease, but it can be a symptom of another condition. Primary amenorrhea occurs when a girl has not had her first period by age 16. Secondary amenorrhea describes women who experience an absence of more than three menstrual cycles after having regular periods.

entries.title: Menstruation and Menstrual Problems
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: The primary sign of menstruation is bleeding from the vagina. Additional signs include cramping, lower back pain, bloating, sore breasts, food cravings, irritability, headache, and fatigue.

entries.title: Cervical Cancer Screening
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: The goal of screening for cervical cancer is to find precancerous cervical cell changes, when treatment can prevent cervical cancer from developing. Sometimes, cancer is found during cervical screening. Cervical cancer found at an early stage is usually easier to treat.

entries.title: Mammograms
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Mammography is an imaging test that uses low-dose x-rays to create pictures of the breast. It is used both to screen for breast cancer and diagnose breast conditions.

entries.title: Screening for Cervical Cancer
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: The HPV test and the Pap test can help prevent cervical cancer or find it early. The HPV test looks for the virus (human papillomavirus) that can cause cell changes on the cervix. The Pap test (or Pap smear) looks for precancers, cell changes on the cervix that might become cervical cancer if they are not treated appropriately.

entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Be aware of urgent maternal warning signs and symptoms during pregnancy and in the year after delivery. Seek medical care immediately if you experience any signs or symptoms that are listed below. The symptoms below can be a sign of a life-threatening condition.

entries.title: Urgent Maternal Warning Signs and Symptoms | HEAR HER Campaign | CDC
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Vaginal bleeding or fluid leaking during pregnancy You have any bleeding from your vagina that is more than spotting—like a period. You have fluid leaking out of your vagina. You have vaginal discharge that smells bad. Vaginal bleeding or discharge after pregnancy You have heavy bleeding—soaking through one or more pads in an hour. You pass clots bigger than an egg or you pass tissue. You have vaginal discharge that smells bad.

entries.title: Urgent Maternal Warning Signs and Symptoms | HEAR HER Campaign | CDC
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)

entries.text: Headache that won’t go away or gets worse over time Feels like the worst headache of your life. Lasts even after treatment with medication and fluid intake. Starts suddenly with severe pain—like a clap of thunder. Throbs and is on one side of your head above your ear. Comes with blurred vision or dizziness. Dizziness or fainting You faint or pass out. You have dizziness and lightheadedness that's ongoing, or comes and goes over many days. You experience a gap in time of which you have no memory.

entries.title: Urgent Maternal Warning Signs and Symptoms | HEAR HER Campaign | CDC

entries.text: Thoughts about harming yourself or your baby You may think about hurting yourself because you: Feel very sad, hopeless, or not good enough. Don't feel that you have control over your life. Feel extremely worried all the time. You may think about hurting your baby and/or you may have scary thoughts that come when you don’t want or that are hard to get rid of.

entries.title: About Folic Acid | Folic Acid | CDC
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: NTDs happen in the first few weeks of pregnancy, often before you know you are pregnant. By the time you realize you're pregnant, it might be too late to prevent an NTD. That is why getting 400 mcg of folic acid before and during early pregnancy is important to help prevent NTDs.

entries.title: About ART | ART | CDC
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: In general, ART procedures involve surgically removing eggs from a woman's ovaries, combining them with sperm in the laboratory, and returning them to a female patient or a gestational carrier. ART also includes egg and embryo cryopreservation (freezing) and egg and embryo donation. The most common type of ART is in vitro fertilization (IVF).

entries.title: Folic Acid | Folate | MedlinePlus
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Folic acid is a B vitamin. It helps the body make healthy new cells. Everyone needs folic acid. For women who may get pregnant, it is really important. Getting enough folic acid before and during pregnancy can prevent major birth defects of her baby's brain or spine. Foods with folic acid in them include: Leafy green vegetables Fruits Dried beans, peas, and nuts Enriched breads, cereals and other grain products If you don't get enough folic acid from the foods you eat, you can also take it as a dietary supplement.

entries.title: Infertility | Infertility Treatments | MedlinePlus
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Infertility means not becoming pregnant after having frequent, unprotected sex for one year or longer. If you are age 35 or older, infertility can be diagnosed after six months. Infertility also includes situations where you can get pregnant, but the pregnancy ends in repeated miscarriage or stillbirth. Infertility is common. It can affect both men and women. Sometimes both partners contribute to the cause.

entries.title: Male Infertility | Infertility | MedlinePlus
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Infertility is a term doctors use if a man hasn't been able to get a woman pregnant after at least one year of trying. Causes of male infertility include: Physical problems with the testicles Blockages in the ducts that carry sperm Hormone problems A history of high fevers or mumps Genetic disorders Lifestyle or environmental factors About a third of the time, infertility is because of a problem with the man. One third of the time, it is a problem with the woman. Sometimes no cause can be found.

entries.title: Gestational Diabetes | MedlinePlus
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: What is gestational diabetes? Some people already have diabetes before they get pregnant. But others may develop diabetes during pregnancy. This type of diabetes is called gestational diabetes. It usually develops around the 24th week of pregnancy. It happens when your body can't make the extra insulin it needs during pregnancy.

entries.title: High Blood Pressure in Pregnancy | MedlinePlus
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
topics: headache that does not go away
entries.text: Preeclampsia can cause other symptoms, including: Too much protein in your urine (called proteinuria). Swelling (edema) in your face and hands. Your feet may also swell, but many women have swollen feet during pregnancy. So swollen feet by themselves may not be a sign of a problem. A headache that does not go away. Vision problems, including blurred vision or seeing spots. Pain in your upper right abdomen (belly). Trouble breathing.

entries.title: Miscarriage | Miscarriage Symptoms | MedlinePlus
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: A miscarriage is an unexpected loss of pregnancy before the 20th week. Most miscarriages happen very early in the pregnancy, often before a woman even knows she is pregnant. What causes a miscarriage? A miscarriage can happen in any pregnancy. Most miscarriages occur because the fetus doesn't develop properly. This is often linked to a genetic problem with the fetus, such as an extra or missing chromosome.

entries.title: Miscarriage | Miscarriage Symptoms | MedlinePlus
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: The signs of a miscarriage may be different for everyone and can vary based on how far along you are in your pregnancy. Signs of a miscarriage can include: Vaginal spotting or bleeding with or without pain. Some women may have some spotting in early pregnancy and don't miscarry. To be sure, contact your provider right away if you have any bleeding.

entries.title: Postpartum Care: MedlinePlus
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Get as much rest as possible. You may find that all you can do is eat, sleep, and care for your baby. And that is perfectly okay. You will have spotting or bleeding, like a menstrual period, off and on for up to six weeks. You might also have swelling in your legs and feet, feel constipated, have menstrual-like cramping. Even if you are not breastfeeding, you can have milk leaking from your nipples, and your breasts might feel full, tender, or uncomfortable. Follow your doctor's instructions on how much activity, like climbing stairs or walking, you can do for the next few weeks.

entries.title: Breastfeeding | Benefits of Breastfeeding | MedlinePlus
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Women who don't have health problems should try to give their babies breast milk for at least the first six months of life. Most women with health problems can breastfeed. There are rare exceptions when women are advised not to breastfeed because they have certain illnesses. Some medicines, illegal drugs, and alcohol can also pass through the breast milk and cause harm to your baby. Check with your health care provider if you have concerns about whether you should breastfeed.

entries.title: Postpartum Depression: MedlinePlus
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Having a baby can be exciting, but it can also be stressful and bring many strong emotions. During the postpartum period, which is the time after you give birth, you may have mood swings, crying spells, or feel anxious. These feelings are common and are often called the postpartum "baby blues". The baby blues usually go away within a few days to a week. If your symptoms are more severe and last longer than two weeks, you may have postpartum depression. Postpartum depression is a common but serious mood disorder that can begin anytime within the first year after childbirth.

entries.title: Pregnancy and Nutrition | MedlinePlus
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: How much weight you should gain depends on your health and how much you weighed before pregnancy: If you were at a normal weight before pregnancy, you should gain about 25 to 35 pounds If you were underweight before pregnancy, you should gain more If you were overweight or had obesity before you became pregnant, you should gain less Check with your provider to find out how much weight gain during pregnancy is healthy for you. You should gain the weight gradually during your pregnancy, with most of the weight gained in the last trimester.

entries.title: Pregnancy | Pregnant | Prenatal Care | MedlinePlus
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Take prenatal vitamins. During pregnancy, you need higher amounts of certain vitamins and minerals, such as folic acid and iron. Be careful with medicines. Always check with your provider before you start or stop any medicine. This includes over-the-counter medicines and dietary or herbal supplements. Stay active. Physical activity can help you stay strong, feel and sleep better, and prepare your body for birth. Check with your provider about which types of activities are right for you. Avoid substances that could hurt your baby, including alcohol, drugs, and tobacco.

entries.title: Trying to conceive
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
topics: how long should we try to conceive
entries.text: You should talk to your doctor about your fertility if: You are younger than 35 and have not been able to conceive after one year of frequent sex without birth control. You are age 35 or older and have not been able to conceive after six months of frequent sex without birth control. You believe you or your partner might have fertility problems in the future (even before you begin trying to get pregnant). You or your partner has a problem with sexual function or libido.

entries.title: Trying to conceive
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
topics: when to have sex to conceive
entries.text: You are most fertile and most likely to get pregnant: Two to three days before your temperature hits the highest point (ovulation) and 12 to 24 hours after ovulation A man's sperm can live for up to three days in a woman's body. The sperm can fertilize an egg at any point during that time. So if you have unprotected sex a few days before ovulation, you could get pregnant.

entries.title: Polycystic ovary syndrome
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
topics: can I get pregnant with PCOS
entries.text: Yes. Having PCOS does not mean you can't get pregnant. PCOS is one of the most common, but treatable, causes of infertility in women. In women with PCOS, the hormonal imbalance interferes with the growth and release of eggs from the ovaries (ovulation). If you don't ovulate, you can't get pregnant. Your doctor can talk with you about ways to help you ovulate and to raise your chance of getting pregnant.

entries.title: Preconception health
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: The five most important things you can do for preconception health are: Take 400 to 800 micrograms (400 to 800 mcg or 0.4 to 0.8 mg) of folic acid every day if you are planning or capable of pregnancy to lower your risk of some birth defects of the brain and spine, including spina bifida. All women need folic acid every day. Talk to your doctor about your folic acid needs. Some doctors prescribe prenatal vitamins that contain higher amounts of folic acid. Stop smoking and drinking alcohol.

entries.title: Preconception health
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Your partner can do a lot to support and encourage you in every aspect of preparing for pregnancy. Here are some ways: Make the decision about pregnancy together. When both partners intend for pregnancy, a woman is more likely to get early prenatal care and avoid risky behaviors such as smoking and drinking alcohol. Screening for and treating sexually transmitted infections (STIs) can help make sure infections are not passed to female partners. Male partners can improve their own reproductive health and overall health by limiting alcohol, quitting smoking or illegal drug use, making healthy food choices, and reducing stress. Studies show that men who drink a lot, smoke, or use drugs can have problems with their sperm.

entries.title: Stages of pregnancy
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: During the first trimester your body undergoes many changes. Hormonal changes affect almost every organ system in your body. These changes can trigger symptoms even in the very first weeks of pregnancy. Your period stopping is a clear sign that you are pregnant. Other changes may include: Extreme tiredness Tender, swollen breasts. Your nipples might also stick out. Upset stomach with or without throwing up (morning sickness) Cravings or distaste for certain foods Mood swings Constipation (trouble having bowel movements) Need to pass urine more often Headache Heartburn Weight gain or loss

Not getting enough iron during pregnancy raises your risk for premature birth or a low-birth-weight baby (less than 5 ½ pounds). Premature birth is the most common cause of infant death. - Getting some exercise
- Taking a hot bath
- Doing relaxation techniques, including yoga and meditation
It may also help to get enough rest and avoid using alcohol and tobacco.

A high-risk pregnancy is one in which you, your fetus, or both are at higher risk for health problems than in a typical pregnancy. But just because you have health problems, it doesn't mean that you, or your fetus, will have a problem during the pregnancy.

entries.title: Rh Incompatibility
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: If you are pregnant and are Rh-negative and your fetus is Rh-positive, it's called Rh incompatibility. Blood from your fetus can cross into your bloodstream, especially during childbirth. If you're Rh-negative and your baby is Rh-positive, your body will react to the fetus's blood as a foreign substance.

entries.title: Rh Incompatibility
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: During your pregnancy, injections of a medicine called Rh immune globulin can keep your body from making Rh antibodies. It helps prevent the problems of Rh incompatibility.

entries.title: Twins, Triplets, Multiple Births
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Women with multiple pregnancies should see their health care providers more often than women who are expecting one baby. Multiple pregnancy babies have a much higher risk of being born prematurely and having a low birth weight. There is also more of a risk of disabilities.

entries.title: Vaccine Recommendations Before, During, and After Pregnancy
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Pregnant women are recommended to get vaccinated against whooping cough, flu, and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). A 2026-2027 COVID-19 vaccine is recommended for all adults ages 18 years and older.

entries.title: Vaccine Recommendations Before, During, and After Pregnancy
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: When a pregnant woman gets a whooping cough vaccine during pregnancy, her body will create protective antibodies and pass some of them to the baby before birth. These antibodies will provide the baby some short-term, early protection against whooping cough. CDC recommends getting a whooping cough vaccine during the 27th through 36th week of each pregnancy, preferably during the earlier part of this time period.

entries.title: Vaccine Recommendations Before, During, and After Pregnancy
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: CDC recommends getting a flu vaccine by the end of October despite flu seasons varying in their timing from season to season. This timing helps protect a pregnant woman before flu activity begins to increase.

entries.title: Safer Food Choices for Pregnant Women
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Pregnant women are more likely to get sick from certain germs spread through food, like Listeria. Some foods are more likely to spread harmful germs, including undercooked meat and eggs, unpasteurized milk and cheese, and unwashed produce. If you are pregnant, choose safer food options to protect yourself and your baby.

entries.title: Medicine and Pregnancy: An Overview
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Almost all pregnant women face decisions about taking medicines during pregnancy. Many need to take medicines during pregnancy to treat health conditions. In some cases, avoiding or stopping a medicine during pregnancy may be more harmful than taking it.

entries.title: Perinatal Depression
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Perinatal depression is a mood disorder that occurs during pregnancy and after childbirth. The symptoms can range from mild to severe. In rare cases, the symptoms are severe enough that a mother and her baby's health and well-being may be at risk.

entries.title: Perinatal Depression
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Women who experience any of these symptoms should see a health care provider. A provider can determine whether the symptoms are due to perinatal depression or something else.

entries.title: Perinatal Depression
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Perinatal depression is a medical condition that can affect any pregnant or postpartum woman, regardless of age, race, ethnicity, income, culture, or education. A woman is not to blame or at fault for having perinatal depression: It is not caused by anything she has or has not done.

entries.summaryEn: Week-by-week guide to how your baby grows and how your body changes, from early pregnancy to birth.

entries.summaryEn: Lists foods and drinks to avoid or limit in pregnancy, including some cheeses, raw eggs, liver and certain fish.

entries.title: Vaccinations in pregnancy
entries.summaryEn: Explains which vaccines are offered in pregnancy, such as flu, whooping cough and RSV, and when to have them.

entries.title: Severe vomiting in pregnancy
entries.summaryEn: Explains hyperemesis gravidarum, how it differs from normal pregnancy sickness, its symptoms, and when to seek help.

entries.title: Pregnancy sickness (nausea and vomiting of pregnancy and hyperemesis gravidarum)
entries.summaryEn: Patient leaflet on pregnancy sickness and hyperemesis gravidarum, covering symptoms, risks and treatment options.

entries.title: Itching in pregnancy
entries.summaryEn: Covers itching in pregnancy and intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy, when to see a GP and how it is treated.

entries.title: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy
entries.summaryEn: Patient leaflet on intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy, including itching, testing, care and what it means for the baby.

entries.title: Vaginal birth after cesarean delivery
entries.summaryEn: ACOG patient FAQ on trying vaginal birth after a previous cesarean, who may be a candidate and the risks.

entries.title: Morning sickness: nausea and vomiting of pregnancy
entries.summaryEn: ACOG patient FAQ on nausea and vomiting in pregnancy, self-care ideas and when it may be hyperemesis.

entries.title: WHO recommendations on antenatal care for a positive pregnancy experience
entries.summaryEn: WHO guideline on routine antenatal care: recommended contacts, tests, nutrition and care aimed at a positive pregnancy experience.

entries.title: Recovering from birth
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Follow your doctor's instructions on how much activity, like climbing stairs or walking, you can do for the next few weeks. Your doctor will check your recovery at your postpartum visit, about six weeks after birth. Ask about resuming normal activities, as well as eating and fitness plans to help you return to a healthy weight.

entries.title: Recovering from birth
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Your period could return in six to eight weeks, or sooner if you do not breastfeed. If you breastfeed, your period might not resume for many months.

entries.title: Postpartum Care
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: You will have spotting or bleeding, like a menstrual period, off and on for up to six weeks. You might also have swelling in your legs and feet, feel constipated, have menstrual-like cramping. Even if you are not breastfeeding, you can have milk leaking from your nipples, and your breasts might feel full, tender, or uncomfortable.

entries.title: Labor and birth
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: C-section is major surgery, and recovery takes about six weeks (not counting the fatigue of new motherhood). In the weeks ahead, you will need to focus on healing, getting as much rest as possible, and bonding with your baby — nothing else. Be careful about taking on too much and accept help as needed.

entries.title: Postpartum depression
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: The baby blues usually go away within a few days. The symptoms of postpartum depression last longer, are more severe, and may require treatment by a health care professional. Postpartum depression usually begins within the first month after birth.

entries.title: Postpartum depression
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Sleep when the baby is sleeping. Don't try to do too much or to do everything by yourself. Ask your partner, family, and friends for help.

entries.title: Common breastfeeding challenges
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Many moms say that their nipples feel tender when they first start breastfeeding. Breastfeeding should feel comfortable once you and your baby have found a good latch and some positions that work.

entries.title: Common breastfeeding challenges
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Don't be worried that your supply is too low to satisfy your baby. Follow your baby's lead. Nursing more and more often will help increase your milk supply.

entries.title: Common breastfeeding challenges
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: A breast infection can happen when other family members have a cold or the flu. It usually happens in only one breast. It is not always easy to tell the difference between a breast infection and a plugged duct, because both have similar symptoms and can get better within 24 to 48 hours.

entries.title: Common breastfeeding challenges
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Ask your doctor for help if you do not feel better within 24 hours of trying these tips, if you have a fever, or if your symptoms get worse. You might need medicine.

entries.title: Common breastfeeding challenges
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: It is normal for your breasts to become larger, heavier, and a little tender when they begin making milk. Sometimes, this fullness may turn into engorgement, when your breasts feel very hard and painful. Engorgement is the result of the milk building up.

entries.title: Making breastmilk
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: You should breastfeed as soon as possible after giving birth. Then, breastfeed your baby every 2 to 3 hours each day so that you will make plenty of milk. This means that in the first few days after birth, your baby will probably need to breastfeed about every one to two hours during the day and a few times at night.

entries.title: Making breastmilk
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Your baby's weight should double in the first few months. Because babies' tummies are small, they need many feedings to grow and be healthy. You can tell if your baby is getting enough milk by the number of wet diapers he has in a day and if he is gaining weight.

entries.title: Making breastmilk
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: The best way to make more breastmilk is to breastfeed often and to empty your breasts completely at each feeding. After emptying your breasts at each feeding, less milk builds up in your breasts between feedings.

entries.title: Making breastmilk
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) recommends breastfeeding as the only source of food for the first 6 months of your baby's life. The AAP also recommends continuing breastfeeding (after starting solid food) beyond your baby's first birthday and for as long as both you and your baby would like.

entries.title: Making breastmilk
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: If you take medicine or are sick, talk to your doctor before you begin breastfeeding. Medicines that are safe for you to take during pregnancy may also be safe while you are breastfeeding. But you should always check with your doctor before you start breastfeeding.

entries.title: How Much and How Often to Breastfeed
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Babies will generally take what they need at each feeding and stop eating when they are full. They should seem content and drowsy after feeding when they have had enough milk. Your baby will breastfeed about 8 to 12 times in 24 hours.

entries.title: Newborn Breastfeeding Basics
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Your baby is steadily gaining weight. It is normal for breastfed babies to lose some weight in the first week following birth. However, they should be back to their birth weight by day 10 to 14 of life.

entries.title: Prescription Medication Use
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Although many medications pass into breast milk, most have little or no effect on milk supply or infant well-being. A few medications should be avoided while breastfeeding. Mothers should talk with their health care provider about medications or supplements they take and medications to avoid.

entries.title: Breast Milk Storage and Preparation
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Freshly expressed or pumped milk can be stored: At room temperature (77°F or colder) for up to 4 hours. In the refrigerator for up to 4 days. In the freezer for about 6 months is best; up to 12 months is acceptable.

entries.title: Pregnant & Postpartum Activity: An Overview
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Get at least 150 minutes (for example, 30 minutes 5 days a week) of moderate-intensity aerobic activity a week during pregnancy and the postpartum period. Remember, some physical activity is better than none, so do what you can.

entries.title: Pregnant & Postpartum Activity: An Overview
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Unless you have a medical reason to avoid physical activity during or after your pregnancy, you can begin or continue moderate-intensity aerobic physical activity.

entries.title: Urinary incontinence
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Problems during labor and childbirth, especially vaginal birth, can weaken pelvic floor muscles and damage the nerves that control the bladder. Most problems with bladder control that happen as a result of labor and delivery go away after the muscles have had some time to heal. If you're still having bladder problems 6 weeks after childbirth, talk to your doctor, nurse, or midwife.

entries.title: Urinary incontinence
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Squeeze the muscles in your genital area as if you were trying to stop the flow of urine or passing gas. Try not to squeeze the muscles in your belly or legs at the same time. Try to squeeze only the pelvic muscles.

entries.title: What are Jaundice and Kernicterus?
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Jaundice is the yellow color seen in the skin of many newborns. Jaundice happens when a chemical called bilirubin builds up in the baby's blood. During pregnancy, the mother's liver removes bilirubin for the baby, but after birth the baby's liver must remove the bilirubin.

entries.title: What are Jaundice and Kernicterus?
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Jaundice usually appears first on the face and then moves to the chest, belly, arms, and legs as bilirubin levels get higher. The whites of the eyes can also look yellow. Jaundice can be harder to see in babies with darker skin color.

entries.title: About Back Sleeping
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: The most effective action that parents and caregivers can take to reduce baby's risk of Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS) and other sleep-related death is to always place baby on their back to sleep, for naps and at night. The back sleep position is the safest sleep position for all babies, including those born preterm and those with reflux, until they are 1 year old.

entries.title: Ways to Reduce Baby's Risk
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Use a sleep surface for baby that is firm (returns to its original shape quickly if pressed on), flat (like a table, not a hammock), level (not at an angle or incline), and covered only with a fitted sheet.

entries.title: Thyroid Disease & Pregnancy
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Postpartum thyroiditis is an inflammation of the thyroid that affects about 1 in 20 women during the first year after giving birth and is more common in women with type 1 diabetes. The inflammation causes stored thyroid hormone to leak out of your thyroid gland. At first, the leakage raises the hormone levels in your blood, leading to hyperthyroidism.

entries.title: Thyroid Disease & Pregnancy
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Symptoms of the hypothyroid phase may be mistaken for the "baby blues"—the tiredness and moodiness that sometimes occur after the baby is born. Symptoms of hypothyroidism may also include trouble dealing with cold; dry skin; trouble concentrating; and tingling in your hands, arms, feet, or legs. If these symptoms occur in the first few months after your baby is born or you develop postpartum depression, talk with your doctor as soon as possible.

entries.title: Pregnancy loss
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: You might feel cheated and angry. Or you might feel extremely sad as you come to terms with the baby that will never be. These emotions are all normal reactions to loss.

entries.title: Pregnancy loss
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Turn to loved ones and friends for support. Share your feelings and ask for help when you need it. Talk to your partner about your loss.

entries.title: Pregnancy loss
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Give yourself plenty of time to heal emotionally. It could take a few months or even a year. Once you and your partner are emotionally ready to try again, confirm with your doctor that you are in good physical health and that your body is ready for pregnancy.

entries.summaryEn: NHS guide to the first days after birth, including how long bleeding (lochia) lasts and what to expect physically.

entries.summaryEn: NHS explanation of the postnatal check at 6 to 8 weeks: what is reviewed and how it fits with the baby's check.

entries.summaryEn: NHS advice on recovering after a caesarean: hospital stay, caring for the wound, stitches and returning to normal activities.

entries.title: Common breastfeeding problems
entries.summaryEn: NHS overview of common breastfeeding problems such as sore nipples, engorgement and mastitis, with advice on getting help.

entries.title: Your menstrual cycle
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: The typical menstrual cycle is 28 days long, but each woman is different. Also, a woman's menstrual cycle length might be different from month-to-month. Your periods are still "regular" if they usually come every 24 to 38 days.

entries.title: About Menstruation
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: The average menstrual cycle is 28 days, but this varies between women and from month to month. In teens, the menstrual cycle can range from 21 to 45 days, but for most women, it is 21 to 35 days.

entries.title: About Menstruation
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: The average menstruation time in normally menstruating women is about 5 days. In the United States, most girls start menstruating shortly after 12 years of age.

entries.title: Your menstrual cycle
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: A girl may start her period anytime between 8 and 15. The first period normally starts about two years after breasts first start to develop and pubic hair begins to grow. The age at which a girl's mother started her period can help predict when a girl may start her period.

entries.title: Your menstrual cycle
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: A girl should see her doctor if: She starts her period before age 8. She has not had her first period by age 15. She has not had her first period within three years of breast growth.

entries.title: Your menstrual cycle
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: For a few years after your first period, menstrual cycles longer than 38 days are common. Girls usually get more regular cycles within three years of starting their periods. If longer or irregular cycles last beyond that, see your doctor or nurse to rule out a health problem, such as polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS).

entries.title: Period problems
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Irregular periods are normal for teenage girls and perimenopausal women. Teen girls' periods may be irregular for the first few years before becoming more regular. During the transition to menopause, called perimenopause, menstrual cycles may become more irregular over time.

entries.title: Your menstrual cycle
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Try to change or rinse your feminine hygiene product before it becomes soaked through or full. Most women change their pads every few hours. A tampon should not be worn for more than 8 hours because of the risk of toxic shock syndrome (TSS)

entries.title: Your menstrual cycle
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Toxic shock syndrome (TSS) is a rare but sometimes deadly condition caused by bacteria that make toxins or poisons. In 1980, 63 women died from TSS. A certain brand of super absorbency tampons was said to be the cause.

entries.title: Your menstrual cycle
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Today, most cases of TSS are not caused by using tampons. But, you could be at risk for TSS if you use more absorbent tampons than you need for your bleeding or if you do not change your tampon often enough (at least every four to eight hours).

entries.title: Period problems
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Unusual or abnormal bleeding is any bleeding that is different from your typical menstrual period or happens when you do not have your period. Causes of unusual bleeding include: Hormonal changes. Changing hormone levels during puberty and perimenopause, the transition to menopause, can cause longer, heavier periods.

entries.title: Period problems
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text:
You should see your doctor if you have unusual bleeding. This may include:
Bleeding after sex, more than once
Spotting or bleeding anytime in the menstrual cycle other than during your period
Bleeding during your period that is heavier or lasts longer than normal
Bleeding after menopause

entries.title: Period problems
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Long-term, severe stress can affect the part of your brain that controls reproduction. As a result, ovulation and your period can stop. Managing the stress can help restore normal menstrual cycles.

entries.title: Stress and your health
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Women who experience chronic or long-term stress may have more severe premenstrual syndrome (PMS) symptoms or irregular periods. Some studies link past abuse or trauma to more severe PMS.

entries.title: Period problems
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Gaining too much weight or losing too much weight can cause missed periods. Menstrual periods will usually restart after losing weight if you are overweight or gaining weight if you are underweight.

entries.title: Acne
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: The menstrual cycle is one of the most common acne triggers. Acne lesions tend to form a few days before the cycle begins and go away after the cycle is completed. Other hormone changes, such as pregnancy and menopause, improve acne in some women.

entries.title: HPV Vaccination
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: HPV vaccination is recommended at ages 11–12 years. HPV vaccines can be given starting at age 9 years. All preteens need HPV vaccination, so they are protected from HPV infections that can cause cancer later in life.

entries.title: HPV Vaccination
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: HPV vaccination provides safe, effective, and lasting protection against the HPV infections that most commonly cause cancer. The HPV vaccine series is most effective when given before a person is exposed to the virus.

entries.title: Urinary Tract Infection Basics
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text:
Symptoms of a bladder infection can include:
Pain or burning while urinating
Frequent urination
Feeling the need to urinate despite having an empty bladder
Bloody urine
Pressure or cramping in the groin or lower abdomen

entries.title: What Is Menopause?
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Menopause describes the stage of a woman's life when her menstrual periods stop permanently, and she can no longer get pregnant. Menopause is not a disease or disorder — it is a normal part of aging for women. The time leading up to menopause is called the menopausal transition or perimenopause.

entries.title: Menopause basics
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Perimenopause is the time before menopause when your hormone levels change. Your periods may become irregular during this time, but you can still become pregnant.

entries.title: Menopause basics
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Perimenopause usually begins in your mid- to late 40s. However, some women notice symptoms in their mid- to late 30s. Perimenopause lasts about four years on average but can last up to 10 years leading into menopause.

entries.title: What Is Menopause?
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Most women begin the menopausal transition between ages 45 and 55, and the process may last for several years. Women reach menopause at different ages, and the average age of menopause is 52 in the United States. You will only know that you've reached menopause when you have not had a period or spotting for a full year.

entries.title: What Is Menopause?
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: During the menopausal transition, the body's production of estrogen and progesterone, two hormones made by the ovaries, declines greatly. Changes in these hormones may explain the symptoms that some women experience during this time. Symptoms related to menopause can last for between two and eight years, though the timing and symptoms are highly variable among women.

entries.title: What Is Menopause?
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: All of these can be normal changes, but to make sure there isn't a problem, see your doctor if: Your periods happen very close together. You have heavy bleeding. You have bleeding or spotting after sex or between periods. Your periods last more than a week. You start bleeding or spotting again after not having a period for more than a year.

entries.title: What Is Menopause?
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: In addition, during the menopausal transition, the body begins to use energy differently. The distribution of fat in the body changes, and women may gain weight more easily. They may also experience changes in their bone density, heart health, body shape and composition, or physical function.

entries.title: Menopause treatment
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Menopause hormone therapy, often just called hormone therapy, can supplement some of the hormones your ovaries no longer make. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved hormone therapies for reducing moderate to severe hot flashes, preventing bone loss and osteoporosis, and relieving vaginal dryness and discomfort.

entries.title: Menopause treatment
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Hormone therapy has risks as well as benefits. Its labeling describes risks such as blood clots, stroke, heart attack, and certain cancers. Your risks depend on your age, health history, and the type, dose, and form of hormone therapy.

entries.title: Heart Disease in Women
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Before menopause, your body makes more estrogen (a female hormone) which helps protect against heart disease. That's why women generally develop coronary artery disease 10 years later than men. During and after menopause, estrogen levels drop and your risk for heart diseases goes up.

entries.title: What Is Menopause?
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: After menopause, women are more vulnerable to certain health conditions, including heart disease, stroke, and osteoporosis. During this time, it is important to continue to eat a healthy diet, stay active, and get enough calcium and vitamin D for optimal bone health.

entries.title: Menopause symptoms and relief
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: In perimenopause, your periods may be shorter or longer, lighter or heavier, or skipped. Vaginal bleeding after 12 months with no period is not normal. See your health care provider right away if you experience this.

entries.title: What Is Menopause?
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: You might feel moodier or more irritable around the time of menopause. Scientists don't know why this happens. It's possible that stress; family responsibilities, such as supporting growing children or caring for aging parents; depression; or feeling extra tired could be causing these mood changes.

entries.title: Menopause symptoms and relief
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: You may feel more irritable, anxious, or experience depression symptoms. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and mindfulness-based stress reduction may help with depression and anxiety during perimenopause and menopause. Talk with your provider about treatment options.

entries.title: What Is Menopause?
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Menopause is a natural process that usually happens on its own as women age. However, menopause can also result from the surgical removal of both ovaries. If you have surgery to remove your ovaries and are not taking hormones, you will stop having periods and may experience symptoms of menopause immediately.

entries.title: Early or premature menopause
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: If you have early or premature menopause, hormone therapy may help relieve symptoms and protect your bones. You and your provider can decide together whether hormone therapy is right for you.

entries.title: Screening for Cervical Cancer
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Your doctor may tell you that you don't need to be screened anymore if: You have had at least three Pap tests or two HPV tests in the past 10 years, and the test results were normal or negative, and You have not had a cervical precancer in the past, or You have had your cervix removed as part of a total hysterectomy for non-cancerous conditions, like fibroids.

entries.title: Sex and Menopause: Treatment for Symptoms
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Some women have vaginal dryness when their bodies experience the menopausal transition. This can make sex painful. Women may also experience a tightening of the vaginal opening, burning, itching, and dryness (called vaginal atrophy).

entries.title: What Is Menopause?
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: For example, smoking is associated with an early onset of menopause and more severe menopausal symptoms.

entries.title: Adult Activity: An Overview
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: According to the current Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, adults need 150 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity a week. This can also be 75 minutes of vigorous-intensity or an equivalent combination of moderate- and vigorous-intensity physical activity. In addition, adults need at least 2 days of muscle-strengthening activity each week.

entries.title: Stress and your health
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Get enough sleep. Most adults need 7 to 9 hours of sleep a night to feel rested.

entries.title: Adult BMI Categories
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: BMI is a calculated measure of body weight relative to height. For adults, BMI categories are underweight, healthy weight, overweight, and obesity. Obesity is further subdivided into three classes.

entries.title: Calcium - Consumer
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: After about age 30, bones slowly lose calcium. In middle age, bone loss speeds up and can lead to weak, fragile bones (osteoporosis) and broken bones. Although bone loss is more common in women, it can affect men too.

entries.title: Vitamin D - Consumer
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Vitamin D is a nutrient you need for good health. It helps your body absorb calcium, one of the main building blocks for strong bones. Together with calcium, vitamin D helps protect you from developing osteoporosis, a disease that thins and weakens the bones and makes them more likely to break.

entries.title: Stress and your health
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: You can take steps to help handle stress in a positive way. Take deep breaths. This forces you to breathe slower and helps your muscles relax.

entries.title: Stress and your health
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Physical activity can relax your muscles and improve your mood. Physical activity also may help relieve symptoms of depression and anxiety. Physical activity boosts the levels of "feel-good" chemicals in your body called endorphins.

entries.title: Stress and your health
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Stress is a reaction to a change or a challenge. In the short term, stress can be helpful. It makes you more alert and gives you energy to get things done.

entries.title: Depression
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Everyone feels sad or low sometimes, but these feelings usually pass. Depression (also called major depression, major depressive disorder, or clinical depression) is different. It can cause severe symptoms that affect how a person feels, thinks, and handles daily activities, such as sleeping, eating, or working.

entries.title: Depression
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text:
Common signs and symptoms of depression include:
Persistent sad, anxious, or "empty" mood
Feelings of hopelessness or pessimism
Feelings of irritability, frustration, or restlessness
Feelings of guilt, worthlessness, or helplessness
Loss of interest or pleasure in hobbies and activities

entries.title: Depression
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Not everyone who is depressed shows all these symptoms. Some people experience only a few symptoms, while others experience many. Depression symptoms interfere with day-to-day functioning and cause significant distress for the person experiencing them.

entries.title: Anxiety Disorders
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Many people worry about things such as health, money, school, work, or family. But anxiety disorders involve more than occasional worry or fear. For people with these disorders, anxiety does not go away, is felt in many situations, and can get worse over time.

entries.title: Generalized Anxiety Disorder: What You Need to Know
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: GAD usually involves a persistent feeling of anxiety or dread that interferes with how you live your life. It is not the same as occasionally worrying about things or experiencing anxiety due to stressful life events. For people with GAD, these feelings of anxiety can last for months or even years.

entries.title: Generalized Anxiety Disorder: What You Need to Know
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text:
People with GAD may:
Worry excessively about everyday things
Have trouble controlling their worries or feelings of nervousness
Feel irritable or "on edge" frequently
Feel restless or have trouble relaxing
Have a hard time concentrating

entries.title: About Water and Healthier Drinks
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Daily water intake recommendations vary by age, sex, pregnancy status, activity level, and breastfeeding status. Daily water intake is mostly from water and other beverages. Foods, especially those with high water content such as many fruits and vegetables, can also add to fluid intake.

entries.title: About Heart Attack Symptoms, Risk, and Recovery
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text:
The major symptoms of a heart attack are:
Chest pain or discomfort. Most heart attacks involve discomfort in the center or left side of the chest that lasts for more than a few minutes or that goes away and comes back.

entries.title: Screening for Breast Cancer
entries.licence: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)
entries.text: Being familiar with how your breasts look and feel can help you notice symptoms such as lumps, pain, or changes in size that may be of concern. These could include changes found during a breast self-exam. Tell your doctor about any changes you notice.
